items.full: About The Author Paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking. He has over 25 years experience working with clients such as Doctors … More about Paul ↬ Weekly tips on front-end & UX . Trusted by 182,000+ folks. You might have already read my name every now and then here at Smashing Magazine. I’m Paul Boag. I’ve written three books with Smashing and 77 articles (yes, I counted), and I sit on Smashing’s advisory board. So when Vitaly and the Smashing team offered me this slot in your inbox, I didn’t take it lightly. I want to tell you about something I’m launching in January with Smashing as my partner , and why I think it matters right now. Every year I talk to hundreds of people working in digital. Some work in-house, some run agencies, and some freelance. And the same thing comes up again and again. The hardest part of the job usually isn’t the design work. It’s everything around it . The stakeholder who redesigns things in the review meeting. The business case sitting in someone’s inbox. The project that has been “about to start” since last spring. And now, the senior manager who has read that AI can do user research in an afternoon. What makes it harder is that a lot of us deal with all this on our own . Many are a team of one, or a team of a few. Their colleagues are great, but they work in the same organization with the same blind spots. Nobody down the corridor has dealt with this before. What’s missing is an outside view . Someone who has dealt with the same awful stakeholder and can tell you how they handled it. Most of us rarely get that conversation, and the job is changing faster than ever. There’s very little established best practice for working with AI yet. Everyone is figuring it out at once, mostly alone. UX Insiders is a small, paid community for people doing UX inside organizations . items.title: OpenAIs GPT-6 Cyber can both break into systems and propose how to fix them
items.desc: With GPT-6 Cyber, OpenAI is introducing an AI model built to find security vulnerabilities in software, develop exploits, and suggest patches. According to OpenAI, it has already found 81 previously unknown vulnerabilities in Firefox and developed 948 working exploits in the Linux kernel, significantly more than its predecessor. The article OpenAIs GPT-6 Cyber can both break into systems and propose how to fix them appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Cyber, an AI model trained specifically to hunt for security vulnerabilities in software. OpenAI says the model can find flaws, build working exploits, and suggest patches. It's also supposed to stay within its assigned boundaries, something some OpenAI models have struggled with in recent months . The firm says it trained GPT-6 Cyber to respect its operational guardrails, using, among other things, a honeypot inspired by the Hugging Face incident . Without any special safety instructions, GPT-6 Cyber avoided boundary violations in 99.93 percent of cases, up from 94.49 percent for its predecessor. With safety instructions enabled, the model stayed within bounds in 100 percent of tests. Overall, OpenAI rates GPT-6 Cyber as "Critical" in the cybersecurity category of its own Preparedness Framework , the same rating it gave to GPT-6 Astra, the "base" model . Ad On ExploitGym, a benchmark that tests whether a model can exploit a given vulnerability in a remote system, GPT-6 Cyber scores 48.5 percent according to OpenAI, compared to 32.1 percent for its predecessor GPT-5.6 Cyber. On a new test for finding vulnerabilities in web apps without access to source code, OpenAI reports a hit rate of 40.3 percent, versus 32.0 percent for GPT-6 Astra, the standard model without cyber training. Ad Full results are available in the system card . All benchmark numbers come from OpenAI itself. No independent testing of the model has been published so far. GPT-6 Cyber has already produced results in real-world security research, according to OpenAI. In a targeted campaign, the model found 81 previously unknown severe vulnerabilities in Firefox , even though the browser had already been tested with earlier AI models. The model also showed that 30 already-known issues were more severe than previously thought. Mozilla accepted the reports and has already shipped fixes. Ad In the Linux kernel, GPT-6 Cyber reproduced 1,724 security vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948 of them, more than five times the 166 that GPT-5.6 Sol managed under the same conditions, according to OpenAI. 304 critical findings were reported to Linux maintainers along with suggested fixes, the company says. For the Linux kernel campaign , OpenAI built a dedicated automated system of scout and analyst agents. They first scanned roughly 5,034 security-relevant locations in the kernel, about seven percent of the total codebase, then filtered those down to 2,308 candidates and confirmed 1,724 vulnerabilities in isolated virtual machines. From there, the system developed the 948 working exploits that OpenAI had already reported. The entire run cost $1,213,430 in compute, according to OpenAI, which works out to $1,279 per exploit. For comparison, programs like Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN have historically paid between $20,000 and $70,000 per comparable finding as a bounty. Ad The agents used at least ten novel attack techniques that were previously unknown even to external kernel security experts, OpenAI says. The article Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong agentic coding results as a fully Apache 2.0 open US model appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: AI chip design firm Ricursive Intelligence has trained an open language model. Ripple-65B Preview was pretrained on 12 trillion tokens and, according to the company, achieved a score of 80.52 on the TerminalBench 2.1 coding benchmark, the best result among open US models. Ripple partly uses Terminus 2 and partly OpenCode as its harness. Other benchmark results show that Ripple does not match the also newly released Inkling 2 Small , but Ripple is likely easier to deploy on users' own hardware. According to Ricursive, total development and training costs amounted to just $32 million, covering all research and development expenses. The model uses a dense Transformer architecture with 65 billion parameters instead of the more common mixture-of-experts approach and is optimized for Nvidia hardware. Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. While Perplexity Computer executes one-off assignments, the new Teammates stay active and work through ongoing projects independently. Each Teammate runs on its own virtual machine with a desktop and browser. Users track progress through dedicated threads in the Perplexity app and can interact with the agents via Slack. items.title: Frontier Radar #5: If AGI is so close, why is everyone leaving? The neolabs and their bets
items.desc: OpenAI is talking about the AGI era, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says AGI has arrived. At the same time, co-creators of today's models are leaving OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Meta to start their own labs, raising billions with no product to show. Why? They're betting that the current recipe alone won't be enough. We've sorted 45 neolabs by their research bets, mapped the limitations of today's AI they're trying to overcome, looked at what's already visible from their work, and explain why Nvidia always wins. items.full: Frontier Radar #5: If AGI is so close, why is everyone leaving? The neolabs and their bets Maximilian Schreiner View the LinkedIn Profile of Maximilian Schreiner Nov 6, 2026 Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER OpenAI is talking about the AGI era, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says AGI has arrived. At the same time, co-creators of today's models are leaving OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Meta to start their own labs, raising billions with no product to show. Why? They're betting that the current recipe alone won't be enough. We've sorted 45 neolabs by their research bets, mapped the limitations of today's AI they're trying to overcome, looked at what's already visible from their work, and explain why Nvidia always wins. Six times a year, THE DECODER's editorial team takes a deep dive into a foundational AI topic in its "Frontier Radar" series, published as a newsletter and exclusively on the site for THE DECODER subscribers . Issue #5 profiles 27 AI labs in detail, sorted by six research bets, plus nearly 20 more in brief and an overview covering origins, valuations, and what's publicly available. Issue #1 covered the current state of agentic AI. Issue #2 examined the measurable impact of AI on productivity. Issue #3 covered the emerging token economy of generative AI. Issue #4 asked what's left of the AI lead over China and where Europe stands. After the launch of GPT-6 Astra, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang declared on X: "AGI has arrived." OpenAI president Greg Brockman called the model a turning point and welcomed humanity to the "AGI era" . What exactly the two men mean isn't clear, since there's no agreed-upon definition of AGI. The message comes through anyway: an extremely powerful AI, possibly a self-improving one, is imminent and the path is mapped out. Many of the people who built today's systems apparently see things differently. Dozens have left the big labs to start their own. Ilya Sutskever co-founded OpenAI and served as its chief scientist; now he's building Safe Superintelligence . Jerry Tworek led the development of OpenAI's reasoning models and now runs Core Automation . David Silver, the mind behind AlphaGo, left Google DeepMind for Ineffable Intelligence . Yann LeCun left Meta after twelve years and founded AMI . Jeff Dean spent 27 years at Google, most recently as chief scientist, and started Discovery Loop . The money follows: Nvidia invested in SSI in July, reportedly five billion dollars according to Bloomberg. The lab hasn't released a single model or paper. Prometheus, Jeff Bezos' industrial AI lab, pulled in twelve billion dollars at a 41 billion valuation in June. Flapping Airplanes has no public model either and raised one billion dollars in an October Series A. The motives are mixed, and not all technical. At these valuations, founders become paper billionaires fast. LeCun left after a strategy dispute with Meta . Sutskever wants to do research without product pressure . Others want to carve out a niche that would be a sideshow at a big lab. Some departures aren't even a clean break: Google itself is a founding investor in Discovery Loop. items.title: The Essential Guide to Proxy Services, Locations, and IP Types
items.desc: Pick a proxy by matching three things: what you are doing, where the IP should appear, and what type of IP you need. A proxy is just a middle stop between you and a website. It hides your real IP and shows another one instead. This matters because IPv4 has only about 4.3 billion possible […]
items.full: Facebook Tweet Pin LinkedIn Pick a proxy by matching three things: what you are doing, where the IP should appear, and what type of IP you need. A proxy is just a middle stop between you and a website. It hides your real IP and shows another one instead. This matters because IPv4 has only about 4.3 billion possible addresses, so clean IPs are limited and valuable [source: ARIN] . TLDR: Use datacenter proxies for speed, residential proxies for trust, and mobile proxies for app-like traffic. Choose the location closest to your target market, such as a US proxy for checking US prices. For example, a retailer testing 500 product pages from 5 countries may use rotating residential proxies to reduce blocks by 30% or more. Do not buy the biggest plan first. Test a small batch. A proxy is like a friendly stunt double for your internet connection. You send a request. The proxy sends it forward. The website sees the proxy IP, not yours. This is useful for many normal tasks. Price tracking. Ad checks. SEO tools. Market research. Social media management. Website testing. Even checking if your site loads correctly in another country. It is not magic, though. Bad proxies get blocked. Slow proxies waste your day. Honestly, it feels like some proxy dashboards were built to make you click seven times just to change one setting. Nobody needs that. Proxy services usually fall into a few buckets. Each one has a job. Location can change everything. A website may show different prices in New York, London, and Berlin. Search results also change by country and city. Ads do too. If you run local SEO checks, use city-level proxies. If you test global pricing, use country-level proxies. If you watch how an app behaves on a mobile network, use mobile proxies from that carrier region. Expect to waste time on weak location filters. Some tools say “US” but give you random states. That can add 10 to 20 seconds per check when you need exact local results. Annoying? Very. There are also different ways proxies can behave. This part matters a lot. For example, use rotating residential proxies when checking thousands of product pages. Use sticky residential proxies when you need to stay logged in for 10 minutes. Use dedicated datacenter proxies when speed matters more than looking human. Start with the task. Do not start with the price page. That is how people end up buying the wrong plan. Also check the provider’s uptime. Many aim for 99% or higher. That sounds nice, but test it yourself. One hour of downtime during a launch can hurt. Some proxy deals look great. Then the pain starts. A good proxy provider should show speed, success rate, location options, and traffic limits. You should also get simple docs. If setup takes an hour for a basic username and password, something is wrong. Proxy services are simple once you split them into three parts: service type, location, and IP behavior . Match those to your task. Test before you scale. Keep records of blocks, speed, and success rates. Your best proxy is not the fanciest one. It is the one that gets the job done without making you mutter at your screen.

items.desc: Fix 404 errors after moving a WordPress blog by installing EPS 301 Redirects, mapping old URLs to new ones, and checking your 404 log daily for the first few weeks. items.full: Facebook Tweet Pin LinkedIn Fix 404 errors after moving a WordPress blog by installing EPS 301 Redirects , mapping old URLs to new ones, and checking your 404 log daily for the first few weeks. WordPress runs a huge share of the web, so even a small migration mistake can create a lot of broken visits fast; W3Techs reports WordPress powers over 40% of all websites [source: W3Techs] . If your old posts, category pages, or media links now show “Not Found,” you do not need to panic. You need clean 301 redirects and a way to catch missed URLs. TLDR: Use EPS 301 Redirects to send old blog URLs to their matching pages on the new domain. For example, redirect olddomain.com/best-coffee-grinders/ to newdomain.com/best-coffee-grinders/ with a permanent 301 rule. On a 300-post blog, even a 5% mismatch means 15 broken posts, which can hurt traffic and annoy readers. Check the plugin’s 404 logs, fix the most visited broken URLs first, and retest everything before you call the migration done. A 404 error means the server cannot find the page being requested. After a WordPress migration, this usually happens because the old URL structure does not match the new one. The common causes are simple, but they are easy to miss: Honestly, it feels like WordPress migrations should catch these problems automatically by now. They do not. A single missed setting can send readers to a dead page instead of your best article. The fastest fix is to add a redirect manager before you start changing random settings. EPS 301 Redirects is built for this job. It lets you create permanent 301 redirects, watch 404 traffic, and route old URLs to the correct new pages. After installing it, go to your WordPress admin area and open the plugin settings. The clean workflow is: For example, if the old post was: https://oldsite.com/top-budget-cameras/ https://newsite.com/best-budget-cameras/ Create a 301 redirect from the old path to the new page. This tells browsers and search engines that the page has moved for good. If your URL structure stayed the same and only the domain changed, you may not need hundreds of manual redirects. A broad rule can forward old paths to the same paths on the new domain. The catch is that wildcard rules can also send bad URLs to bad places. If your old site had messy slugs, test first. Do not redirect every broken URL to the homepage. That may look neat in reports, but it gives readers a poor experience and can confuse search engines. EPS 301 Redirects helps because it shows which URLs are still hitting 404 pages. This is where you find the mess migration tools missed. Start with the most repeated errors. If one broken URL appears 80 times in a week, fix that before a URL that appeared once. Expect to waste time on odd cases, like uppercase letters, old campaign links, or image files from five years ago. It is annoying, but the log makes the work clear. Sometimes the right redirects exist, but WordPress still throws 404 errors. In that case, refresh the permalink rules. Go to Settings > Permalinks . Do not change anything yet. Click Save Changes . items.title: State propaganda in some Chinese AI models is only "a thin layer" that fine-tuning can strip away
items.desc: Nous Research retrained Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B to produce Arete-27B, largely stripping out its pro-Chinese bias. The propaganda rate dropped from 22 percent to less than one percent, while general capabilities remained intact in tests. The method relied on 53 million tokens of supervised fine-tuning. The political bias is "applied late, it is applied thin," the team writes. The article State propaganda in some Chinese AI models is only "a thin layer" that fine-tuning can strip away appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Nous Research fine-tuned Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B on 53 million tokens to strip out Chinese state propaganda. The resulting model, Arete-27B, drops its propaganda rate from 22 percent to under one percent while keeping general capabilities intact. Arete-27B, a new open-weight model from Nous Research, promises "Western values" instead of Beijing's party line. The US startup, best known for its open-source agent Hermes , fine-tuned Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B to get there. According to Nous , Chinese open-weight models rank among the strongest available but carry state-mandated behavior baked into their weights. With Qwen3.8-27B, the team observed refusals, evasive answers, and responses aligned with the Chinese Communist Party. Ad Nous built its own test with 803 prompts across seven categories, including free speech, state ideology, education, privacy and surveillance, democracy, and the environment. For each prompt, the team defined two to four facts drawn from a dated source article: laws, news reports, or research papers. Ironically, the politically right-leaning Grok 4.7 from Elon Musk's xAI serves as the judge model, checking whether a response mentions, omits, or contradicts those facts. Ad A response counts as propaganda when it reproduces Beijing's official narrative instead of the facts, endorses it, or presents it as an equally valid perspective. The judge must cite the specific wording and doesn't know which model wrote the answer. Unmodified Qwen3.8-27B scored 2.32 out of 5 on factual accuracy, and 22 percent of its answers contained propaganda. Western models like Mistral Large 4 or Gemma 4 31B came in below one percent, while GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash landed at 15 and 16 percent. Nous chose Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab as its teacher model because an open model wouldn't break terms of service that ban distillation. Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra was also on the shortlist, but Nous says there were signs of irregularities on China-related topics. The team suspects the bias carried over from training on Chinese open-weight models and reports similar contamination in its own projects. Thinking Machines itself used models including the Chinese Kimi K2.5 for Inkling's synthetic training data. Ad Nous trained Qwen3.8-27B with supervised fine-tuning on about 53 million tokens over two epochs, without reinforcement learning or preference optimization. The team says it removed overlaps between training and test prompts beforehand. Arete-27B scores 2.98 on factual accuracy, and the share of propagandistic answers drops to 0.9 percent. The biggest shift showed up in the free speech category, where the fact score jumped from 0.89 to 2.44 and the propaganda rate fell from 60 to one percent. With reasoning mode turned on, Arete reaches 3.07, though that number is based on only two of five runs so far. Ad General capabilities don't suffer, according to Nous. On the company's internal Hermes Bench, Arete-27B hits 65.60 percent compared to 65.77 percent for the base model. items.title: Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar
items.desc: The "Into the Unknown" benchmark tasks nine AI agents with tackling open research questions from U.S. national laboratories. None of the 135 submissions meets all requirements. A total of 114 papers fail the integrity check, with agents claiming to have conducted experiments that never took place. GPT-6 Astra performs best but still doesn't meet the experts' standards. The article Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar Jonathan Kemper View the LinkedIn Profile of Jonathan Kemper Nov 7, 2026 Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER A new benchmark puts AI agents to work on open research questions from US national labs. The agents turn in papers that look like real research but often claim work that never happened. Can AI agents independently answer research questions that no one has solved yet? A team led by researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, working with scientists from US Department of Energy national labs, built a benchmark called "Into the Unknown" to find out. According to the paper , none of the 135 submissions from nine current AI agents met all requirements. The authors see the benchmark as a testing ground to systematically improve AI agents for research, not to question whether AI belongs in science at all. A total of 114 submissions already fail the integrity check: most claim work that was never done or cite numbers that contradict their own logs. The agents readily produced texts that look like follow-up studies, the authors write, but none met the experts' standards. Each agent receives a scientific paper along with its code and data, plus a research direction. Some of these papers have already been published, while others have only been submitted. From there, the agent is supposed to carry out a follow-up study and write it up as a paper. The 15 tasks come from ten researchers across quantum computing, plasma physics, chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning. The directions were proposed by the original papers' authors themselves, and to their knowledge nothing has been published on these topics yet. Open research poses a basic problem: there's no answer key. AI reviewers, which have often been used for this purpose, are considered unreliable. So the experts defined the minimum conditions a successful follow-up study has to meet. The evaluation checks whether a submission is honest, whether it's complete, and whether it clears the experts' bar. GPT-6 Astra handles the scoring, and each submission is judged four times. The agents tested were Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3. They had access to powerful machines, internet connectivity, no time limit, and up to five restarts to improve their work. In total, they ran for nearly 2,000 hours. Just three agents managed submissions without integrity violations: GPT-6 Astra on 11 of 15 tasks, GPT-5.6 Sol on six, and Claude Opus 5.5 on four. Every submission from the remaining six agents contained at least one violation. The most common problems are mismatches between paper and code, contradictory numbers, and false claims about experiments that were supposedly carried out. Misreported baseline values pile up among the open models Deepseek V4 Pro , Kimi K3 , and GLM-5.3 . Two submissions with hardcoded rather than computed results came from Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3. items.full: A Google Research AI can detect signs of high blood pressure using a regular smartwatch, with no blood pressure cuff needed for calibration. The AI relies on two sensors already built into modern watches—a pulse sensor and a motion sensor—according to a Google blog post . The study was published in Nature . A neural network learned from nearly 500,000 hours of sensor data by comparing short segments and figuring out which ones belonged to the same person, picking up typical pulse and heartbeat patterns without any diagnoses to guide it. The system then averages these patterns over several days and calculates a probability for high blood pressure. Google's health model SensorFM also learns from smartwatch data. In a study of 196 people across five US research sites, the watch spotted hypertension about as well as a traditional cuff, identifying 65.8 percent of those with high blood pressure compared to 55.3 percent for the standard in-office measurement. Ad Google says the findings have been folded into the blood pressure trends feature in the Google Health app, but the method is still a research project and doesn't replace a diagnosis. The goal is to nudge people toward getting checked. More than half of people with high blood pressure don't know they have it, according to Google.
